topics: 🤱 Rabbi Yehuda's Second Offspring — 'exists' only where it creates a stringency, never a leniency
🐑 The Paschal Offering Brought in Impurity — reconciling a puzzling baraita about a woman after childbirth
💰 Sliding-Scale Offerings: Three Tiers — wealth, poverty, and extreme poverty across five different cases
🧮 Calculating the Value of a Peruta Offering — the Gemara's careful math on how cheap an offering can be
👥 Maidservant vs. Every Other Forbidden Relation — five ways her case diverges from the rest

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Settling a Doctrine, Then Pricing an Offering
overview.subtitle: Keritot 10a–10b
overview.hebrewSource: יֵשׁ מֵבִיא בְּדַלּוּת וַעֲשִׁירוּת, וְיֵשׁ מֵבִיא בְּדַלּוּת וְיֵשׁ מֵבִיא בְּדַלֵּי דַלּוּת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf resolves the previous daf's open question: does Rabbi Yehuda treat a woman's 'second' overlapping birth or miscarriage as though it truly happened, or as though it didn't? Through a series of proofs from baraitot about the Paschal offering and about counting purification days, the Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yehuda applies this fiction only when it creates a stringency for the woman, never when it would grant her a leniency. The Gemara then returns to the mishna's sliding-scale offerings, cataloging exactly what each of the five relevant transgressors brings at each level of wealth, working out through careful arithmetic just how little an offering can be worth. The daf closes with a new mishna cataloging five ways the case of an espoused maidservant diverges from every other forbidden relation.

slides.title: 🤱 Rabbi Yehuda's Second Offspring: Stringency Only
slides.subtitle: A chain of proofs settles how far his legal fiction extends

nodes.content: ❓ Does Rabbi Yehuda's 'second offspring is as though nonexistent' rule (for offerings) also apply to ritual purity — and if so, does it ever work in the woman's favor?

🐑 Rav Huna's proof attempt from a Paschal-offering baraita is redirected: Rav Ḥisda reads it as two sons born on consecutive days, so 'day 40' is really day 41 of the first — testing whether the second birth delays her purity
📜 Multiple baraitot on 'sixty days,' 'thirty days,' and 'six days' each independently teach that her count must be entirely continuous — never interrupted or dispersed by an intervening birth
🔍 Each of these continuity-verses only makes sense according to Rabbi Yehuda, since the Rabbis already count purely from the second birth without dispersal

✅ Conclusion: Rabbi Yehuda's fiction that the second offspring 'doesn't exist' applies only for stringency (delaying her offering) — for purity, where nonexistence would be a leniency, he treats the second birth as fully real and interrupting

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: A legal fiction in halakha is never applied uniformly for its own sake — its scope is fixed by which direction, stringent or lenient, the underlying law actually points.

slides.title: 💰 Sliding-Scale Offerings: Three Tiers
slides.subtitle: A baraita spells out exactly what each transgressor brings, based on wealth
rows: Wealthy: lamb + bird. Poor: bird (sin) + bird (burnt) — one bird instead of the lamb
Guilt offering (lamb) is fixed either way; wealthy adds lamb + ewe, poor substitutes two birds
Oath of testimony / utterance of the lips / defiling the Temple
Wealthy: ewe or goat. Poor: two birds. Extremely poor: one-tenth ephah of flour (a meal offering)

callout.label: Pattern:
callout.text: Sometimes one offering replaces one (bird for lamb), sometimes two replace two, sometimes two replace one, and sometimes one replaces two — the Gemara uses this variety to work out the actual monetary values involved.

slides.title: 🧮 Calculating the Value of a Peruta Offering
slides.subtitle: How cheap can the extreme-poverty meal offering really be?

steps.content: 1️⃣ A guilt offering ram must be worth 2 sela (Lev. 5:15); therefore a lamb (used in poverty tiers) is worth 1 sela
2️⃣ The historical nest-price crisis (daf 8) shows a poverty-tier bird-pair cost a quarter-dinar — 1/16th of a sela's value
3️⃣ Rava: the whole calculation is better anchored to a woman after childbirth, whose single bird is worth 1/32 of a lamb (rather than the 1/16 ratio used for the other sliding-scale cases)

4️⃣ Applying that same 1/32 ratio one level further down (extreme poverty relative to poverty) yields a value just under one peruta — rounded up, since the Torah does not sanction an offering worth less than a peruta

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: This math establishes just how minimal the Torah's leniency toward poverty can go — down to the smallest coin in circulation, but never lower.

slides.title: 👥 Maidservant vs. Every Other Forbidden Relation
slides.subtitle: A new mishna: five ways intercourse with an espoused maidservant diverges from all other forbidden relations

boxes.title: All other forbidden relations
items: Unwitting violation brings a sin offering (a female animal)
Man and woman are equally liable for lashes and for an offering
Even the initial stage of intercourse (ha'meareh) is treated like full completion — liable for each act separately

boxes.title: The espoused maidservant
items: Unwitting violation brings a guilt offering (a male animal)
Only the woman receives lashes; only the man brings an offering — the two are never equal
Liability requires a completed act; multiple acts with her collapse into a single offering (as taught on daf 9)

callout.label: The mishna's framing:
callout.text: The Torah imposed a stringency on the maidservant case regarding repeated acts (only full completion counts, and even so, one offering covers many), while treating the punishment and offering structure far more leniently than for other forbidden relations.

slides.title: 🐑 Whose Case Explains the Paschal-Offering Baraita?
slides.subtitle: A challenging baraita about a woman after childbirth eating the Paschal offering while still technically impure

lines.speaker: Rav Huna
lines.text: A baraita states: one slaughters and sprinkles the Paschal offering's blood on behalf of a woman after childbirth on day 40 (for a male) or day 80 (for a female) — proof that Rabbi Yehuda treats her as pure enough by then!

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: But she's still impure that night and cannot eat sacrificial food until day 41/81 — how could she eat the Paschal offering?

lines.speaker: Rav Ḥisda
lines.text: The baraita describes two sons born on consecutive days — 'day 40' is really day 41 relative to the first son, so she qualifies through the first birth's timeline.

lines.speaker: Further test
lines.text: If Rabbi Yehuda held the second birth interrupts purity even for leniency, this reading collapses — so the baraita only works if his fiction is stringency-only, confirming the daf's earlier conclusion.

lines.speaker: Rava's alternative
lines.text: Proposes instead that this is a Paschal offering brought while the community is impure — permitted even for those normally excluded, once they've immersed, though a 'lacking-atonement' status still limits some until nightfall of the qualifying day.

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: Multiple competing readings of one baraita all converge on confirming how narrowly Rabbi Yehuda's legal fiction actually operates.

summary.principle: Rabbi Yehuda's rule that an overlapping second birth 'does not exist' applies only where it stringently delays a woman's offering, never where it would leniently interrupt her purification count; and the Torah's sliding-scale offerings, precisely priced down to the peruta, show how far halakha accommodates genuine poverty without ever waiving an offering altogether.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's conclusion, when does Rabbi Yehuda treat an overlapping 'second' birth or miscarriage as though it truly exists?
o: Always, for every purpose
Only when it creates a stringency (delaying the offering); when it would create a leniency for purity, he treats it as nonexistent
Never — he always treats it as nonexistent
Only on Yom Kippur
quiz.e: The Gemara concludes from several baraitot requiring a continuous, undispersed day-count that Rabbi Yehuda's fiction that the second offspring 'doesn't exist' applies only where it produces a stringency, not where it would produce a leniency.

quiz.q: According to the baraita, what does a woman after childbirth bring if she is in a state of poverty?
o: Two lambs
One bird as a sin offering and another bird as a burnt offering, substituting for the lamb
Nothing at all
A meal offering only
quiz.e: In poverty, a woman after childbirth brings two birds — one as her sin offering (as she would even in wealth) and a second bird replacing the lamb burnt offering required of a wealthy woman.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's calculation, roughly what is the minimum monetary value of the meal offering brought by someone in a state of extreme poverty (dalei dalut)?
o: A full sela
A quarter-dinar
About one peruta, the smallest coin, since the Torah does not sanction an offering worth less
It has no minimum value at all
quiz.e: Working from the values of a lamb, a ram, and a woman after childbirth's bird offering, the Gemara calculates the extreme-poverty offering at just under a peruta, rounded to one peruta since a lesser value would be improper.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what is one key difference between intercourse with an espoused maidservant and intercourse with other forbidden relations?
o: The maidservant case requires no offering at all
Unwitting relations with a maidservant require a guilt offering (a male animal), while other forbidden relations require a sin offering (a female animal)
Only maidservants receive the death penalty
Both cases treat men and women identically
quiz.e: The mishna teaches that unlike other forbidden relations, which require a sin offering, intercourse with an espoused maidservant requires a guilt offering — and a guilt offering is specifically a male animal, unlike the female animal of a sin offering.

quiz.q: Regarding the initial stage of intercourse (ha'meareh), how does the maidservant case differ from other forbidden relations according to the mishna?
o: Both treat it identically as full liability
For other forbidden relations, the initial stage alone creates liability like full completion; for the maidservant, only a fully completed act creates liability
The maidservant case has no concept of ha'meareh
Only completed acts count in both cases
quiz.e: The mishna teaches that for other forbidden relations, even the initial stage of intercourse is treated as equivalent to a completed act for liability purposes, but for the maidservant, liability requires a fully completed act.
